The closure itself is documented (at the outbreak of war in 1939 Chanel shut her couture house, keeping only the boutique for perfume and accessories, and put some 3,000 to 4,000 mostly female staff out of work), but it cannot be told honestly apart from what followed. Archival work summarised in Hal Vaughan's Sleeping with the Enemy (2011) and in AFP's 2021 reporting (FashionUnited, 'Strong whiff of wartime scandal clings to Coco Chanel') records that she spent the occupation at the Ritz with the German intelligence officer Hans Guenther von Dincklage, was registered by the Abwehr in 1941 as agent F-7124 ('Westminster'), went to Berlin in 1943 in connection with the Modellhut peace-feeler scheme, and tried to use the Nazi 'Aryanisation' laws to take back her perfume rights from her Jewish partners, the Wertheimers. Told truthfully, these facts would take over a 280-380-word story, and no reflection addressed to the reader could follow them without either moralising or treating collaboration and antisemitism as a lesson in resilience. The closure's motive is also contested: her own stated reason was that it was no time for fashion, while several biographers link it to the 1936 sit-in strike by her workers; under the rule to attribute blame only as courts, regulators or the founder put it, the story could give only her own account, which would read as a whitewash. Sources also disagree on the date (at the declaration of war in September 1939, about three weeks later, or, in the 2021 AFP-based report, after Paris was occupied in 1940), on the number laid off (over 3,000 versus up to 4,000) and on the comeback year (1953 versus 1954). The Met's essay on Chanel, the most authoritative general source found, returned HTTP 429 to automated requests. No other Chanel episode was substituted, because the comeback and earlier episodes either lead into the same wartime record or were not the assigned closure arc.
